summary: Defines a channel binding type called tls-exporter that works with TLS 1.3, following the channel binding framework in RFC 5056. It also changes the default channel binding to the new type for TLS versions above 1.2, and updates RFC 5801, RFC 5802, RFC 5929, and RFC 7677. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A channel binding glues a login to the exact secure tunnel it was done in, so nobody can slip it into another tunnel. This gives TLS 1.3 a proper glue.

questions: how do channel bindings work with tls 1.3
what is channel binding in tls
subtitle: A way to tie a login to the exact TLS 1.3 connection it runs over, using exported keying material.

tldr.problem: The older tls-unique channel binding was found to be open to the triple handshake vulnerability, and it is not defined for TLS 1.3, so TLS 1.3 had no channel binding.
tldr.mechanism: A new binding type, tls-exporter, takes 32 bytes of exported keying material from the TLS connection using the label EXPORTER-Channel-Binding and an empty context.
tldr.outcome: tls-exporter becomes the default channel binding over TLS 1.3 and later for SCRAM and GS2, and the mandatory-to-implement one whenever channel binding is implemented for TLS 1.3.

today: RFC 9266 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 5801, RFC 5802, RFC 5929 and RFC 7677.

sections.title: Why TLS 1.3 Needs a New Binding
sections.content:
A channel binding ties an authentication exchange to the secure channel it runs over. The tls-unique type from RFC 5929 was found to be susceptible to the triple handshake vulnerability unless the extended master secret extension of RFC 7627 is used.

TLS 1.3 uses a complete transcript hash, similar to the extended master secret procedures. Even so, the safety of channel bindings with TLS 1.3 was not analyzed as part of the core protocol work, so RFC 8446 left them unspecified. RFC 9266 fills that gap by adding tls-exporter to RFC 5929, replacing some usage of tls-unique.
sections.eli5: The old way of gluing a login to a tunnel had a hole, and the newest kind of tunnel had no glue at all. This RFC makes new glue that fits.

sections.title: How tls-exporter Is Computed
sections.content:
The binding uses Exported Keying Material (EKM), which TLS implementations already widely expose. The EKM comes from the keying material exporters of RFC 5705 and Section 7.5 of RFC 8446, called with three inputs.

  • Label: the ASCII string EXPORTER-Channel-Binding, with no terminating NUL.
  • Context value: a zero-length string.
  • Length: 32 bytes.

The mechanism is defined only when the TLS handshake results in unique master secrets. That is always true for TLS 1.3, and true for earlier versions when the extended master secret extension is in use.
sections.eli5: Both ends of the tunnel run the same recipe on a secret they share and get the same 32-byte code. The code is like a stamp that only this tunnel can make.

sections.title: SCRAM and GSS-API over SASL
sections.content:
The specifications for SCRAM (RFC 5802, RFC 7677) and for GSS-API mechanisms in SASL (RFC 5801) name tls-unique as the default channel binding over TLS. Because tls-unique is not defined for TLS 1.3 and greater, RFC 9266 updates those documents to make tls-exporter the default over TLS 1.3 and greater.

It also makes tls-exporter the mandatory-to-implement channel binding if any channel bindings are implemented for TLS 1.3: implementations that support channel binding over TLS 1.3 MUST implement it. The default for SCRAM over TLS 1.2 does not change and is still tls-unique.
sections.eli5: Programs that log in over a tunnel used to pick the old glue by default. For the newest tunnels they now pick the new glue, and anyone who supports glue there must support this one.

sections.title: Uniqueness and Legacy TLS
sections.content:
The binding is built so that disclosing it does not leak secret information about the TLS channel or affect its security. The derived data MUST NOT be used for any purpose other than channel binding, and in particular MUST NOT be used as a secret key to protect privileged information.

The binding gives only the weaker kind of uniqueness from RFC 5056: it identifies the TLS connection, not the upper-layer authentication protocol instance. So applications MUST NOT use it for more than one authentication mechanism instance on a given TLS connection, and MUST immediately close the connection when the upper-layer protocol ends.

It can be used with TLS below 1.3 only with care to ensure unique master secrets. When TLS renegotiation is enabled on a connection, tls-exporter is not defined for it and implementations MUST NOT support it. Users who want channel binding should upgrade to TLS 1.3 or later.
sections.eli5: The code only says which tunnel you are in, so use it for one login and then close the tunnel. Do not reuse it as a password.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered tls-exporter in the Channel-Binding Types registry as a unique type for TLS, with the note that the channel binding is not secret and the intended usage is COMMON. The description is the EKM value obtained from the current TLS connection.

IANA also added the exporter label EXPORTER-Channel-Binding to the TLS Exporter Labels registry, marked DTLS-OK and Recommended.
sections.eli5: The new glue and the name of its recipe were written in the official lists so nobody else picks the same names.
